# Worker launch and imports

These techniques cover worker-start concurrency, safe import reuse and process-bootstrap boundaries. Open this topic when serial starts or repeated imports delay the first batch, bootstrap re-imports construct trainers again, or inherited thread locks block workers.

[Catalog index](../../technique_catalog.md) · [Startup](../startup.md)

**`bounded_parallel_worker_spawn`: start independent spawn workers concurrently**
- Trigger: A loader launches worker processes in a loop, waiting for each start call before starting the next. PyTorch `DataLoader` does this regardless of `multiprocessing_context` and has no public option for concurrent launch. The start method changes the cost of each launch, not the loop: `spawn` can repeat imports and serialize the dataset for every worker, compounding the startup cost (see `spawn_mmaps_by_descriptor`). `fork` can avoid that serialization, but is not a safe shortcut when the parent has active threads or initialized accelerator state.
- Technique: add configurable, bounded concurrent worker starts to the existing launcher, with independent process state for every worker. Limit effective startup concurrency to the smaller of the configured cap and worker count; select the cap from peak CPU and memory across all ranks on the host. Keep worker IDs, seeds, queues, restored worker state, sample order and steady-state worker count unchanged. Keep serial startup as the generic default, make concurrency opt-in and allow explicit per-loader settings to take precedence. Parallel startup does not itself change the process-start method: assess any switch from `forkserver` to `spawn` separately.
- Guards: large caps can saturate host CPU, and the best cap varies with hardware; leave CPU and memory headroom rather than targeting maximum concurrency. Make enablement and fallback selection consistent across distributed ranks. Wrapper and adapter APIs must explicitly consume or forward the loader-only option, not leak it through arbitrary kwargs into a datasource. Concurrent parent-side serialization must be thread-safe: lock one-time shared-storage materialization so every worker inherits stable storage and descriptors. Serialize memmaps as backing-directory metadata and reopen them read-only in the child, close temporary descriptors, and do not mutate live parent objects in serialization hooks. These serialization safeguards address both observed races and preventive memory/lifetime risks, not a measured speedup from each safeguard. Preserve failure cleanup and resume behavior, retain a serial fallback and watch for low-frequency startup failures. Preloading accelerator-initializing modules into a forkserver can make inherited accelerator state unsafe. Measure startup and whole-run time separately; a small slowdown in a tiny-job comparison was consistent with startup noise, not evidence of a coordination-cost mechanism.

**`preloaded_forkserver_workers`: amortize safe CPU imports in a worker template**
- Trigger: each spawned loader worker repeats heavy CPU-side dataset or transform imports.
- Technique: where the process runtime supports it, configure a loader-only forkserver context and its preload list before starting the server or any loader workers. The preload list should contain audited CPU-only modules whose imports finish in a quiescent state; import them once in the clean server template, then create loader children from that template so they can inherit already-imported read-only state. Keep the training ranks on their existing safe spawn topology. In each child, initialize worker-specific clients, handles, seeds, and mutable transform state after creation rather than in the template. Check transitive imports as well as the named modules for accelerator initialization, threads, and native runtime state; a nominally CPU module can still import unsafe dependencies. Compare first-batch time and host peak memory with the existing method and retain a spawn fallback for modules that cannot safely be preloaded. Preloading reduces repeated import work only for state that is safe to inherit.
- Guards: preload no accelerator state, live clients, background threads, or thread-owning native runtimes. Confirm imports are quiescent and worker-specific state is initialized in children. Accelerator-initializing preloads failed in related startup work. Preserve deterministic seeds and backing-file ownership; retain a safe fallback for incompatible modules.

**`fork_safe_worker_bootstrap`: guard launches and keep threads out of the fork window**
- Trigger: worker bootstrap re-imports a launcher and constructs trainers again, inherited thread-held locks deadlock forked workers, or non-fork bootstrap spends excessive time pickling the dataset and re-importing dependencies.
- Technique: put process creation and trainer construction behind `if __name__ == "__main__":`, and fail early with that remedy if trainer construction occurs during bootstrap re-import. Scope a PyTorch loader's start method with its `multiprocessing_context` rather than changing the whole process. A clean `forkserver` avoids inheriting the threaded trainer's locks; with default preloading, a script run by path is re-imported once in the server rather than in each spawned worker. Where compatibility checks permit `fork` to avoid serialization/import overhead, defer continuous prefetch until after worker creation, join running prefetch threads before sampler changes, and consider keeping validation workers alive across epochs. These are different workload-specific choices, not a universally preferred start method.
- Guards: a main guard does not make inherited locks safe, and CPU-only workers can still deadlock when forked from a threaded parent. Check native-runtime and accelerator compatibility before considering fork; stopping one known prefetch thread is not a general fork-safety proof. Set `multiprocessing_context` only when `num_workers > 0`. Clean bootstraps can still pay per-worker serialization/import costs. In one tested case, switching to fork was bundled with dataset-memory, padding and crop changes, so do not attribute the full result to the start method. A forkserver comparison had only short single-device and distributed smoke validation. Keep worker seeding, main-process pinning and teardown intact.
